description:
We are a team of passionate innovators, engineers, and problem-solvers united by our love for science, technology, and space exploration.

We’re bringing together our creativity, technical skills to tackle real-world challenges and develop innovative solutions. We believe that everyone has great ideas, and we’re here to prove that with teamwork, determination, and ingenuity, even the sky isn’t the limit.
summary: We developed an interactive, web-based 3D terrain viewer and Martian traverse planner built with Three.js using real NASA HiRISE elevation models of Gale Crater. The application directly addresses the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge by combining high-resolution orbital terrain data, slope-aware pathfinding, rover and astronaut simulation modes, and dynamic environmental factors like atmospheric dust opacity and solar time into a single unified interface. This tool is important because it bridges the gap between complex scientific datasets and practical mission planning, providing students, educators, and future explorers with an accessible, immersive platform to evaluate Martian terrain hazards, test navigation routes, and visualize surface conditions for safer and more effective exploration
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

The Hispanic Martians Mars Viewer is an interactive, web-based 3D terrain visualization and mission traverse planner built for the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge[cite: 17]. Powered by real planetary elevation data from Gale Crater, Mars—specifically NASA HiRISE stereo Digital Terrain Models (ESP_040770_1755) and orthoimages—the application generates an accurate, navigable 3D Martian landscape directly in the browser. Explorers can interact with the environment across multiple operational modes: driving a physics-simulated rover with real-time telemetry, switching to an astronaut first-person perspective equipped with a dynamic flashlight and WebXR (VR/AR) support, and planning safe extravehicular activity (EVA) routes using an integrated A* pathfinding algorithm that calculates terrain slope risks and hazards. Additionally, the platform layers environmental datasets directly onto the map, allowing users to simulate Martian solar time, view dynamic diurnal temperature and radiation curves, and play back historical atmospheric dust opacity events such as the 2018 global dust storm.

What benefits does it have?

The platform bridges the gap between complex, raw scientific datasets from the NASA Planetary Data System (PDS) and intuitive, real-time mission planning. Rather than analyzing static 2D elevation charts or isolated weather logs in separate tools, users can view topography, slope gradients, atmospheric dust opacity, and solar angles simultaneously in a single unified interface. For human explorers or mission planners, this integrated approach speeds up route verification, improves hazard awareness during Marswalks, and demonstrates how environmental shifts directly affect surface visibility and operational safety.

What is the intended impact of the project?

Our intended impact is twofold: first, to prototype a unified, multi-layered navigation and environmental awareness interface tailored for future human missions to Mars; and second, to make open NASA planetary science accessible to students, educators, and the global public. By turning authentic orbital telemetry and rover atmospheric records into an interactive browser experience that requires no specialized GIS software, the project lowers the barrier to exploring planetary geology and encourages broader engagement in STEM and space exploration.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

We developed the application using standard, lightweight web technologies—HTML5, CSS3, and modern JavaScript (ES6+)—to ensure accessibility across desktop and mobile devices. For 3D terrain rendering, camera controls, lighting, and immersive headsets, we used Three.js (v0.128.0) alongside OrbitControls and WebXR APIs. During development and local testing, we used Python to run local HTTP servers and process terrain elevation grids. Our data pipeline integrates NASA HiRISE stereo Digital Terrain Models and orthoimages (ESP_040770_1755), NASA Planetary Data System (PDS) Curiosity atmospheric opacity records, NASA Mars Trek references, and USGS Astrogeology mapping resources.

How is your project creative?

Instead of treating a Martian map as a static topographic model, we designed a living, dynamic mission simulator that connects orbital mapping with surface-level human experience. Users can transition seamlessly from a high-altitude orbital overview down to an Entry, Descent, and Landing (EDL) Sky Crane deployment sequence, and immediately begin a surface traverse on foot or by rover. Combining automated slope-aware A* pathfinding with real-time Martian solar time, dynamic temperature and radiation plotting, and historical dust storm playback transforms raw planetary telemetry into an engaging, story-driven survival and exploration tool.

What factors did your team consider?

Scientific integrity and transparency were primary considerations. We ensured that elevation profiles, terrain meshes, and slope-based pathfinding constraints are derived directly from measured NASA HiRISE DTM data, while clearly distinguishing simulated surface shaders and modeled diurnal weather curves from raw orbital imagery. We also prioritized cross-platform accessibility and performance—optimizing 3D mesh rendering for standard web browsers and designing a responsive interface with touch controls, virtual directional pads, and mobile safe-area compliance so anyone can explore Gale Crater on a phone, laptop, or VR headset.
